content: Endometrial cancer, which originates from the lining of the uterus, is the seventh most common cancer affecting women globally. Hormonal therapy has been proposed as a potentially beneficial treatment for patients with advanced or recurrent forms of this cancer. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the indications, effectiveness, and safety of hormonal therapy in such cases. To conduct this evaluation, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL, up to May 2009. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of relevant studies, and consultations with experts in the field were also utilized. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adult women diagnosed with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer who received hormonal therapy. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently conducted by two reviewers. The analysis was restricted to single-trial comparisons, and no meta-analyses were performed due to the heterogeneity of the data. Six trials, encompassing a total of 542 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These trials investigated the use of hormonal therapy as a single agent, as part of combination therapy, and at varying doses (low versus high). The findings revealed no evidence that hormonal therapy, whether used alone or in combination with other treatments, improved overall survival or five-year disease-free survival in women with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. However, low-dose hormonal therapy appeared to offer a potential benefit in terms of overall survival and progression-free survival (PFS) when compared to high-dose therapy. Specifically, the hazard ratio (HR) for overall survival was 1.31 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04 to 1.66), and the HR for PFS was 1.35 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.71). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of hormonal therapy, in any form or dose, or as part of combination therapy, to improve survival outcomes in patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. Importantly, none of the included RCTs had a sufficient sample size to detect a significant survival benefit. Given the lack of proven survival advantage and the variability in patient populations, the decision to use hormonal therapy should be individualized, with the primary goal being palliation of the disease. Future research should consider whether endpoints such as quality of life, treatment response, or symptom relief should take precedence over overall survival and PFS as the primary objectives of clinical trials.
